overview.about: World Meteorological Day marks the founding of the World Meteorological Organization and celebrates the role of weather and climate science in protecting lives and livelihoods. Each year it adopts a theme highlighting a facet of meteorology and its importance to society.
overview.nextEvent: The next World Meteorological Day is marked on 23 March by national weather services and the WMO around a chosen theme. It underscores the value of forecasting, early warnings and climate monitoring worldwide.

@graph.name: World Meteorological Day
@graph.description: The World Meteorological Organization marks its founding convention each 23 March and uses the day to connect weather, climate and water science with everyday decisions. Forecasts, warnings and climate records rely on national meteorological services sharing observations across borders. The observance is a useful reminder that a forecast is more than a weather icon: it is infrastructure for farmers, pilots, emergency teams and families deciding when to travel. Following the day means looking for the year’s official WMO theme, local science events and practical explanations of how early warnings reduce harm when dangerous weather develops.

exploreIntro: These places illustrate different weather and climate contexts: Australia combines heat, coasts and drought, Kenya depends on seasonal rainfall, and Switzerland makes Alpine snow, glaciers and forecasting visible.
participationIntro: Use the day to make weather and climate information easier to understand:

participationSteps.text: Read or share a trusted weather, climate or early-warning explainer.
Check how your local alert system works for storms, heat, floods or other hazards.
Use the day in education or workplace communication to explain why forecasts and observations matter.
Credit meteorological services and avoid reposting unsourced weather claims.
